items.title: Sperry's Nobel work showed hemispheres process independently
items.claim: Roger Sperry's split-brain research (Nobel 1981) found that when the corpus callosum is severed and images shown to only one visual field, what happens?

options.text: Both hemispheres still share all information
An object shown only to the left visual field (right hemisphere) cannot be named verbally (because language is typically left-hemisphere lateralised) but can be selected by touch with the left hand

items.reveal_title: Hemispheres can act independently after callosotomy
items.reveal:
Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga studied epilepsy patients who had undergone callosotomy. Their experiments showed each hemisphere could process information without conscious awareness in the other, raising deep questions about the unity of consciousness.

The popular 'left-brain logical, right-brain creative' caricature is wildly oversimplified — both hemispheres contribute to most cognitive tasks in intact brains. Lateralisation is real but localised to specific functions (language, visuospatial processing).
items.why: Findings about rare clinical populations can constrain theories of normal cognition. The popular interpretation often outruns the evidence.

items.title: Vygotsky's ZPD emphasised social learning
items.claim: Lev Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development (work in 1920s-30s, popularised in West from 1962 onwards) describes:

options.text: The gap between what a child can do alone and what they can do with help from a more knowledgeable other — emphasising social context as constitutive of cognitive development
A physical region of the brain
A stage of motor development only

items.reveal:
Vygotsky died in 1934 aged 37. His work was suppressed in Stalin's USSR and reached the West in translation (Thought and Language, 1962; Mind in Society, 1978).

'Scaffolding' was Bruner's term (Wood, Bruner & Ross 1976) capturing the temporary support that enables a learner to reach beyond independent ability. Modern educational applications: peer tutoring, guided discovery, gradual release of responsibility models.
items.why: Vygotsky's emphasis on social context contrasts with Piaget's relatively solitary child. Modern developmental psychology integrates both — children develop through cultural participation, not despite it.

items.title: The Strange Situation has cultural biases
items.claim: Van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg's 1988 meta-analysis of Strange Situation studies across 8 countries found what pattern?

options.text: Identical proportions of attachment types in all cultures

Higher rates of insecure-avoidant in Germany and insecure-resistant in Japan and Israel — but interpretation is contested: are these real attachment differences or measurement artefacts of an American-developed procedure?
The Strange Situation cannot be administered outside the US
No cultural variation exists in any developmental measure

items.reveal:
Takahashi (1990) noted Japanese infants are rarely left alone, so the Strange Situation may induce extreme distress that registers as 'resistant'. German samples (Grossmann) showed avoidance interpreted differently — culturally valued early independence.

IJzendoorn's later work (1999, 2008) emphasised within-culture variation often exceeds between-culture. The procedure's validity outside Western middle-class contexts remains debated.
items.why: Standardised procedures developed in one culture may measure different things in another. Cross-cultural psychology often needs methodological adaptation, not just translation.
